cases.title: Toddler age and vocabulary size
cases.context: A study was reported concerning early word learning. For 10 toddlers, a parent filled out a vocabulary checklist (a list of common words on which the parent marks every word the child says). The table below shows the age of each toddler in months (mo) and the expressive vocabulary size (number of different words the child says). Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. The summations are Σx = 226, Σx² = 5290, Σ(x − x̄)² = 182.4, Σy = 1754, Σy² = 414524, Σ(y − ȳ)² = 106872.4, Σxy = 43969 and Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 4328.6.
tasks: Calculate the slope b and the intercept a of the regression line of vocabulary size on age. DO NOT use R. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Write the regression line and state in a single complete sentence what the slope says about these toddlers.
cases.symbols: \(n\) (number of toddlers), \(x\) (age, mo), \(y\) (vocabulary size, words), \(b\) (least-squares slope, words/mo), \(a\) (least-squares intercept, words), \(\bar x,\bar y\) (sample means), \(D\) (shared denominator).

steps.title: Collect the sums
steps.words: The least-squares formulas need only these five numbers. Here x is age and y is vocabulary size.

steps.title: Calculate the shared denominator
steps.words: Both the slope formula and the full intercept formula divide by this quantity.

steps.title: Calculate the slope
steps.words: The slope is the estimated increase in mean vocabulary size for each additional month of age, in words/mo.

steps.title: Calculate both sample means
steps.words: The least-squares line passes through the point of means (22.6 mo, 175.4 words).

steps.title: Calculate the intercept from the means
steps.words: The unrounded slope is carried into this step, because rounding b first would shift the intercept.

steps.title: Check the intercept with the full formula
steps.words: Both routes give the same intercept, in words.

steps.title: Write the line and check the slope with the deviation sums
steps.words: The deviation form of the slope gives the same value. The intercept is negative because the line is extended far below the youngest age that was sampled, so it is not a vocabulary size that a child could have.

cases.conclusion: The least-squares line is \(\hat y=-360.9+23.73x\). Between 16 and 30 months of age, mean vocabulary size is estimated to rise by about 23.73 words for each additional month.

cases.title: Speaking rate and voice onset time
cases.context: In a study looking at how talkers adjust their consonants when they speak faster, 10 adult speakers read a list of words beginning with the sound p. For each speaker, the speaking rate in syllables per second (syll/s) and the mean voice onset time (VOT, the time between the release of the lips and the start of vocal fold vibration) in milliseconds (ms) were measured. The data are listed in the table below. Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. The summations are Σx = 44.4, Σx² = 208.88, Σ(x − x̄)² = 11.744, Σy = 659, Σy² = 44629, Σ(y − ȳ)² = 1200.9, Σxy = 2814.2 and Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = −111.76.
tasks: Find the linear regression relationship between speaking rate (independent variable) and VOT (dependent variable). DO NOT use R. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Write the regression line and state what the sign of the slope says about VOT in faster speech.
cases.symbols: \(n\) (number of speakers), \(x\) (speaking rate, syll/s), \(y\) (voice onset time, ms), \(b\) (least-squares slope, ms per syll/s), \(a\) (least-squares intercept, ms), \(\bar x,\bar y\) (sample means), \(D\) (shared denominator).

steps.title: Collect the sums
steps.words: The least-squares formulas need only these five numbers. Here x is speaking rate and y is voice onset time.

steps.title: Calculate the shared denominator
steps.words: Both the slope formula and the full intercept formula divide by this quantity.

steps.title: Calculate the slope
steps.words: The slope is negative. It is the estimated change in mean VOT for each additional syllable per second.

steps.title: Calculate both sample means
steps.words: The least-squares line passes through the point of means (4.44 syll/s, 65.9 ms).

steps.title: Calculate the intercept from the means
steps.words: The unrounded slope is carried into this step, because rounding b first would shift the intercept.

steps.title: Check the intercept with the full formula
steps.words: Both routes give the same intercept, in ms.

steps.title: Write the line and check the slope with the deviation sums
steps.words: The deviation form of the slope gives the same value. The intercept is the height of the line at a speaking rate of zero, which lies outside the range of the data.

cases.title: Age and oral reading speed in school children
cases.context: Researchers interested in reading development did a study to evaluate how oral reading speed changes during the school years. Twelve children read a grade-level passage aloud, and the reading speed in words per minute (wpm) was recorded together with the age of each child in years (yr). The data are listed in the table below. Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. The summations are Σx = 114, Σx² = 1118, Σ(x − x̄)² = 35, Σy = 1364, Σy² = 166782, Σ(y − ȳ)² = 11740.67, Σxy = 13581 and Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 623.
tasks: Calculate the slope b of the regression line of reading speed on age, and then estimate the scatter about the line of means \(s_{y|x}\). DO NOT use R.
Calculate the standard errors \(s_b\) and \(s_a\). Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
cases.symbols: \(s_{y|x}\) (standard error of the estimate, wpm), \(s_x,s_y\) (sample SDs), \(b\) (slope), \(s_b\) (SE of the slope, wpm/yr), \(s_a\) (SE of the intercept, wpm), \(\bar x\) (mean age), \(n\) (sample size).

steps.title: Calculate the slope from the deviation sums
steps.words: Reading speed is estimated to rise by 17.8 words per minute for each additional year of age.

steps.title: Calculate the sample variances
steps.words: The supplied sums of squared deviations are divided by n − 1 to give the sample variances of age and of reading speed.

steps.title: Square the pieces inside the shortcut
steps.words: The first term is the total variance of reading speed. The second term is the part of that variance explained by the line.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the estimate
steps.words: The factor (n−1)/(n−2) converts the n−1 denominators of the sample variances into the n−2 denominator required for regression. Children of the same age scatter about the line with an SD of about 8.1 words per minute.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the slope
steps.words: The slope is known to within a standard error of about 1.36 words per minute per year.

steps.title: Evaluate the bracket for the intercept
steps.words: The second term is large because the mean age lies far from x = 0, where the intercept is defined.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the intercept
steps.words: The intercept is far less precise than the slope because it is an extrapolation to an age of zero.

steps.title: Check with the sum of squared residuals
steps.words: The sum of squared residuals about the line gives the same standard error of the estimate, so the shortcut is confirmed.

cases.conclusion: The slope is 17.8 wpm/yr and the scatter about the line is \(s_{y|x}=8.07\) wpm. The standard errors are \(s_b=1.364\) wpm/yr and \(s_a=13.17\) wpm.
cases.answerName: Standard error of the estimate s_y|x

cases.title: Age and P300 latency in children
cases.context: In a study looking at brain development, 11 children and adolescents performed an auditory oddball task (a rare high tone had to be counted among frequent low tones) while the electroencephalogram (EEG) was recorded. The table below shows the age of each participant in years (yr) and the latency of the P300 (a positive EEG wave that follows the rare tone) in milliseconds (ms). Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. The summations are Σx = 121, Σx² = 1441, Σ(x − x̄)² = 110, Σy = 4369, Σy² = 1747537, Σ(y − ȳ)² = 12249.64, Σxy = 46926 and Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = −1133.
tasks: Calculate the slope b and the intercept a of the regression line of P300 latency on age. DO NOT use R. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Based on your calculations for b, is the trend between P300 latency and age statistically significant?
What are the 95% confidence intervals for the slope and for the intercept of the line of means?

hypotheses.nullWords: There is no linear trend between P300 latency and age in children and adolescents, so the slope of the line of means is zero.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Mean P300 latency changes linearly with age in children and adolescents, so the slope of the line of means is not zero.

cases.symbols: \(b\) (sample slope), \(s_b\) (SE of the slope), \(a\) (sample intercept), \(s_a\) (SE of the intercept), \(s_{y|x}\) (standard error of the estimate), \(\beta\) (population slope), \(\alpha_{LOM}\) (population intercept), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom), \(t_\alpha(\nu)\) (two-tailed critical value).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: Use the t test for the slope of a regression line. The null states that mean P300 latency does not change with age.

steps.title: Calculate the slope and intercept
steps.words: The slope is negative. Mean P300 latency is estimated to fall by 10.3 ms for each additional year of age.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the estimate
steps.words: Participants of the same age scatter about the line with an SD of about 8 ms.

steps.title: Calculate the coefficient standard errors
steps.words: Here \(s_x=3.316625\) yr and \((n-1)s_x^2\) equals the supplied sum 110.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: Under the null, β = 0, so the statistic is the slope divided by its standard error.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom
steps.words: Two coefficients were estimated from the data.

steps.title: Find the 0.05 critical value
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 9, two-tailed column 0.05. The printed cutoff is 2.262.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: The size of the statistic exceeds the cutoff, so the null hypothesis of no trend is rejected.

steps.title: Find the P range
steps.words: Row 9, column 0.001 prints 4.781. The statistic exceeds the largest printed cutoff, so P < 0.001.

steps.title: Construct the 95% interval for the slope
steps.words: The interval contains only negative values and does not contain 0, which agrees with the test.

steps.title: Construct the 95% interval for the intercept
steps.words: The intercept is the height of the line at an age of zero, which is far outside the ages that were sampled.

cases.conclusion: The trend between P300 latency and age is statistically significant, because |t| = 13.46 with ν = 9 exceeds \(t_{0.05}(9)=2.262\) (P < 0.001). There is evidence that mean P300 latency is shorter in older children, by about 10.3 ms for each additional year of age. The 95% confidence interval for the slope is −12.03 to −8.569 ms/yr and does not contain 0. The 95% confidence interval for the intercept is 490.7 to 530.3 ms.

cases.title: Morning cortisol and digit span
cases.context: Researchers interested in stress and working memory did a study with 10 university students during an examination week. A saliva sample was taken in the morning to measure cortisol (a stress hormone) in nanomoles per liter (nmol/L). Each student then completed a digit span test (the longest list of digits that can be repeated back in the correct order). The data are listed in the table below. Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. The summations are Σx = 139.4, Σx² = 2056.92, Σ(x − x̄)² = 113.684, Σy = 63, Σy² = 405, Σ(y − ȳ)² = 8.1, Σxy = 865.9 and Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = −12.32.
tasks: Calculate the slope b and the intercept a of the regression line of digit span on cortisol. DO NOT use R. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
Based on your calculations for b, is the trend between digit span and cortisol statistically significant? Use a significance level of α = 0.05 for your inference.
What are the 95% confidence intervals for the slope and for the intercept of the line of means?

hypotheses.nullWords: There is no linear trend between digit span and morning cortisol in students, so the slope of the line of means is zero.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Mean digit span changes linearly with morning cortisol in students, so the slope of the line of means is not zero.

cases.symbols: \(b\) (sample slope), \(s_b\) (SE of the slope), \(a\) (sample intercept), \(s_a\) (SE of the intercept), \(s_{y|x}\) (standard error of the estimate), \(\beta\) (population slope), \(\alpha_{LOM}\) (population intercept), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom), \(t_\alpha(\nu)\) (two-tailed critical value).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: Use the t test for the slope of a regression line. The null states that mean digit span does not change with cortisol.

steps.title: Calculate the slope and intercept
steps.words: The sample slope is slightly negative, about one tenth of a digit per nmol/L.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the estimate
steps.words: Students with the same cortisol level scatter about the line with an SD of about 0.92 digits.

steps.title: Calculate the coefficient standard errors
steps.words: Here \(s_x=3.55409\) nmol/L and \((n-1)s_x^2\) equals the supplied sum 113.684.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: Under the null, β = 0, so the statistic is the slope divided by its standard error.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom
steps.words: Two coefficients were estimated from the data.

steps.title: Find the 0.05 critical value
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, two-tailed column 0.05. The printed cutoff is 2.306.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: The size of the statistic is smaller than the cutoff, so the null hypothesis of no trend is not rejected.

steps.title: Find the P range
steps.words: The statistic does not reach the 0.20 column of row 8, so P is well above 0.05.

steps.title: Construct the 95% interval for the slope
steps.words: The interval contains 0, which agrees with the test. A slope of zero is consistent with these data.

steps.title: Construct the 95% interval for the intercept
steps.words: The intercept interval does not contain 0. This only says that the line is well above zero digits at a cortisol level of zero.

cases.conclusion: The trend between digit span and cortisol is not statistically significant, because |t| = 1.257 with ν = 8 is smaller than \(t_{0.05}(8)=2.306\) (P > 0.05). These data do not provide evidence that digit span changes with morning cortisol. The 95% confidence interval for the slope is −0.3073 to 0.09051 digits per nmol/L and contains 0. The 95% confidence interval for the intercept is 4.958 to 10.66 digits.

cases.title: Age and the 4 kHz hearing threshold
cases.context: A study was reported concerning hearing in adults who had worked in a noisy factory. For 10 workers, the pure-tone hearing threshold at 4 kilohertz (kHz) was measured in the better ear with an audiometer. The threshold is the quietest tone that can be heard, in decibels hearing level (dB HL), so a higher value means worse hearing. The table below shows the age of each worker in years (yr) and the threshold. Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. The summations are Σx = 600, Σx² = 37182, Σ(x − x̄)² = 1182, Σy = 325, Σy² = 12125, Σ(y − ȳ)² = 1562.5, Σxy = 20800 and Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 1300.
tasks: Find the linear regression relationship between age (independent variable) and hearing threshold (dependent variable), and the scatter about the line \(s_{y|x}\). DO NOT use R. Make sure to show your intermediate calculations.
What is the 95% Confidence Interval for the mean hearing threshold at an age of 65 yr?
What is the 95% Confidence Interval for an observation of hearing threshold at an age of 65 yr?
cases.symbols: \(\hat y\) (predicted mean), \(s_{\hat y}\) (SE of the predicted mean), \(s_{Y_{new}}\) (SE for one new worker), \(s_{y|x}\) (scatter about the line), \(\bar x\) (mean of x), \(s_x\) (SD of x), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: Calculate the regression line
steps.words: The mean threshold is estimated to rise by about 1.1 dB for each additional year of age.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the estimate
steps.words: Workers of the same age scatter about the line with an SD of about 4.1 dB.

steps.title: Calculate the predicted value
steps.words: This is the estimated mean threshold of workers aged 65 yr, in dB HL. No worker in the sample is exactly 65 yr old, so the value comes from the line.

steps.title: Evaluate the distance term
steps.words: The second term grows with the distance between 65 yr and the mean age of 60 yr.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the mean prediction
steps.words: This standard error describes the uncertainty in the height of the line at x = 65.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom and cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, two-tailed column 0.05. The printed cutoff is 2.306.

steps.title: Construct the interval for the mean
steps.words: With 95% confidence, the mean threshold of all such workers aged 65 yr lies between about 34.73 and 41.27 dB HL.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error for one new worker
steps.words: The scatter of single values about the line is added to the uncertainty in the line itself.

steps.title: Construct the interval for one worker
steps.words: This interval should contain the threshold of a single randomly chosen worker aged 65 yr with 95% confidence.

steps.title: Compare the two widths
steps.words: The observation interval is about 3 times as wide, because single workers scatter about the mean even if the line were known exactly.

cases.conclusion: The predicted threshold at 65 yr is 38 dB HL. The 95% confidence interval for the mean threshold at 65 yr is 34.73 to 41.27 dB HL. The 95% confidence interval for the threshold of one worker aged 65 yr is 28.05 to 47.94 dB HL, which is much wider.
cases.answerName: Lower endpoint of the mean-threshold CI at 65 yr

Ten young adult listeners were each randomly assigned to a different speech rate in syllables per second (syll/s). The word recognition score (percentage of words repeated back correctly) was recorded for each listener. The data are listed in the table below. Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. steps.title: Calculate the regression line

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the estimate

cases.title: Slow-wave sleep and overnight word-pair retention (R output)
cases.context: Researchers interested in sleep and memory did a study in which 18 adults learned a list of word pairs in the evening and were tested the next morning. Slow-wave sleep (SWS, the deepest stage of sleep) was measured in minutes (min) with overnight polysomnography (a sleep recording of brain waves, eye movements and muscle tone). Retention was the percentage of word pairs still recalled in the morning. The R command lm(Retention.pct ~ SWS.min) gives the coefficients below, a residual standard error of 5.043 on 16 degrees of freedom, and multiple R-squared 0.3745. The SWS values total 1592 min, with Σx² = 148854 min².

Give the correlation coefficient.

cases.title: Male versus female rats: amphetamine dose and locomotor activity
cases.context: In a study looking at sex differences in the response to a stimulant, 16 male and 16 female rats were each randomly assigned to one dose of amphetamine between 0.5 and 4.0 milligrams per kilogram of body weight (mg/kg). Locomotor activity (number of infrared beam breaks in an open cage during 10 minutes) was then counted. Separate regressions of activity on dose were fitted to the two groups with lm() in R, and the output is summarized in the table. In each group the doses total 36 mg/kg with Σx² = 102, giving a mean of 2.25 mg/kg and an SD of 1.183 mg/kg.
tasks: Using the R output, is there evidence that the slope of activity on dose is different in male and female rats? Please state how you reached your conclusions.
Apply the corresponding test to the intercepts.

hypotheses.nullWords: Locomotor activity rises with amphetamine dose at the same rate in male and female rats (equal slopes of the two lines of means).
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The rate at which locomotor activity rises with amphetamine dose is different in male and female rats.

cases.symbols: \(b_M,b_F\) (male and female slopes), \(s_{b_M},s_{b_F}\) (their SEs), \(s_{b_M-b_F}\) (SE of the slope difference), \(a_M,a_F\) (intercepts), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: Use the two-regression-line t test. Both slopes are significant on their own in the R output (t = 10.030 and 12.606), so the comparison is meaningful.

steps.title: Calculate the slope difference
steps.words: The order males minus females is kept throughout, so the difference is negative.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the difference
steps.words: The equal-n formula applies because both groups have 16 rats. The two standard errors are read from the Std. Error column of the Dose rows.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: The difference is about 2.6 standard errors below zero.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom
steps.words: Each line uses up two degrees of freedom for its intercept and slope.

steps.title: Compare with the 0.05 cutoff
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 28, two-tailed column 0.05. The size of the statistic exceeds the cutoff, so equal slopes are rejected.

steps.title: Find the P range
steps.words: The statistic lies between the 0.02 and 0.01 columns of row 28, so 0.01 < P < 0.02.

steps.title: Apply the corresponding intercept test
steps.words: Replacing slopes by intercepts in the same formula gives |t| = 0.12 < 2.048, so the intercepts do not differ significantly. The two lines start at about the same activity at a dose of zero and then separate.

cases.conclusion: There is a difference between the slopes, because |t| = 2.572 with ν = 28 exceeds \(t_{0.05}(28)=2.048\) (0.01 < P < 0.02). In these data, activity rises faster with dose in female rats (135.7 beam breaks per mg/kg) than in male rats (98.26 beam breaks per mg/kg). The intercepts do not differ significantly.
rOutput: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
Residual standard error: 44.89 on 14 degrees of freedom
Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
Residual standard error: 49.33 on 14 degrees of freedom

cases.title: Years of musical training and pitch discrimination
cases.context: A study was reported concerning musical training and hearing. Ten adults each completed a pitch discrimination test, in which two tones are played and the listener says which one is higher. The discrimination threshold (the smallest pitch difference that is heard reliably) was recorded in cents (hundredths of a semitone), so a smaller value means finer pitch hearing. The table below shows the threshold and the number of years (yr) of formal musical training. Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use. The summations are Σx = 62, Σx² = 608, Σ(x − x̄)² = 223.6, Σy = 324, Σy² = 11976, Σ(y − ȳ)² = 1478.4, Σxy = 1459 and Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = −549.8.
tasks: Calculate the correlation (Pearson coefficient) between discrimination threshold and years of musical training. DO NOT use R.
Is the correlation different from zero? Give the P range.

hypotheses.nullWords: There is no linear relationship between years of musical training and the pitch discrimination threshold in the population (the population correlation is zero).
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Years of musical training and the pitch discrimination threshold are linearly related in the population (the population correlation is not zero).

cases.symbols: \(r\) (sample correlation coefficient), \(\rho\) (population correlation), \(b\) (slope), \(n\) (number of pairs), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: Calculate r from the deviation totals
steps.words: The units cancel, so r has no units. The sum of cross products is negative, so r is negative.

steps.title: Check with the slope relation
steps.words: The slope is about −2.46 cents per year of training, and r has the same sign as b.

steps.title: Square r
steps.words: About 91% of the variation in the discrimination threshold is accounted for by the linear relationship with years of training.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: This statistic equals the slope statistic b divided by its standard error for the same data.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom and the 0.05 cutoff
steps.words: Start with α = 0.05. Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, two-tailed column 0.05.

steps.title: Decide and give the P range
steps.words: The size of the statistic exceeds every printed cutoff in row 8, so the null hypothesis of zero correlation is rejected with P < 0.001.

steps.title: Interpret r
steps.words: A value this close to −1 indicates a strong negative linear relationship. Musicians with more years of training tend to have smaller (better) discrimination thresholds.

cases.conclusion: The correlation is r = −0.9563. The correlation is different from zero, because t = −9.246 with ν = 8 is larger in size than \(t_{0.001}(8)=5.041\) (P < 0.001). In these data, adults with more years of musical training hear smaller pitch differences.

questions.stem: Using the supplied summations for the 10 toddlers, what is the least-squares slope b of vocabulary size on age?
options: \(8.312\) words/mo
\(23.73\) words/mo
questions.why: The slope is (10·43969 − 226·1754)/(10·5290 − 226²) = 43286/1824 = 23.73 words/mo. Dividing Σxy by Σx² skips the correction for the means, and dividing by Σ(y − ȳ)² gives the slope of age on vocabulary.
equations: b=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}

questions.stem: For the 10 speakers, the slope of VOT on speaking rate is \(b=-9.516\) ms per syll/s. What is the intercept a?
questions.why: a = ȳ − b x̄ = 65.9 − (−9.516)(4.44) = 108.2 ms. Subtracting a negative product adds it. Adding the negative product instead gives 23.65 ms, and rounding b to −10 first gives 110.3 ms.

questions.stem: For the 12 school children, \(s_{y|x}=8.07\) wpm and \(s_x=1.784\) yr. What is the standard error of the slope \(s_b\)?
questions.why: s_b = (1/√11)(8.07/1.784) = 1.364 wpm/yr. Leaving out 1/√(n−1) gives 4.524, dividing by 11 instead of √11 gives 0.4113, and using s_x² gives 0.7647.

questions.stem: In a study of 10 students, the regression of digit span on morning cortisol gives |t| = 1.26 for the slope, and the printed cutoff is \(t_{0.05}(8)=2.306\). Which conclusion is correct?
options: The slope is exactly zero, so cortisol has no effect on digit span.
The trend is significant because the slope is negative.
The trend is not statistically significant, so these data do not provide evidence that digit span changes with cortisol.
The test cannot be done because n is smaller than 30.
questions.why: |t| is smaller than the cutoff, so the null hypothesis of zero slope is not rejected. Failing to reject does not prove that the slope is zero. It only means that these data do not show a trend.

questions.stem: For the 10 listeners, the line predicts \(\hat y=76.92\)% at 6.8 syll/s, with \(s_{\hat y}=1.039\) and \(s_{y|x}=3.119\). What is the lower endpoint of the 95% confidence interval for the score of one new listener at 6.8 syll/s?
questions.why: For one observation, s_Ynew = √(3.119² + 1.039²) = 3.288, and 76.92 − 2.306(3.288) = 69.34%. Using s_ŷ alone gives the interval for the mean (74.52%), and 1.96 is not the cutoff for ν = 8.

questions.stem: The R output gives a slope of 98.262 (Std. Error 9.796) for 16 male rats and 135.69 (Std. Error 10.76) for 16 female rats. What is the t statistic for the difference in slopes (males minus females)?
questions.why: With equal n, the SE of the difference is √(9.796² + 10.76²) = 14.55, so t = −37.43/14.55 = −2.572. Adding the two standard errors without squaring gives −1.821, and dividing by only the male standard error gives −3.821.

questions.stem: For the 10 adults, Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = −549.8, Σ(x − x̄)² = 223.6 and Σ(y − ȳ)² = 1478.4. What is the Pearson correlation between discrimination threshold and years of musical training?
questions.why: r = −549.8/√(223.6·1478.4) = −0.9563. The sign comes from the sum of cross products, so r is negative. The value −2.459 is the slope, which keeps its units, and −0.9144 is r² with a minus sign.

questions.stem: An audiologist fits a regression of hearing threshold on age. A new patient aged 60 yr arrives, and the audiologist wants a range that should contain this one patient's threshold with 95% confidence. Which standard error belongs in the interval?
options: \(s_{Y_{new}}=\sqrt{s_{y|x}^2+s_{\hat y}^2}\), because one patient scatters about the line
\(s_{\hat y}\), because the line gives the mean at 60 yr
\(s_b\), because the slope carries the uncertainty
\(s_y/\sqrt n\), the standard error of the mean threshold
questions.why: An interval for one new observation must include the person-to-person scatter about the line as well as the uncertainty in the line. The interval built with s_ŷ only covers the mean threshold of all patients aged 60 yr, so it is too narrow for one patient.

questions.stem: Vocabulary size is regressed on age separately for 14 children raised with one language and 14 children raised with two languages. The question is whether vocabulary grows at a different rate in the two groups. Which statistic and degrees of freedom are used?
options: An unpaired t test on mean vocabulary size, with ν = 26
\(t=b_1/s_{b_1}\) for each group, each with ν = 12
A paired t test on the 14 pairs of children, with ν = 13
questions.why: A different rate of growth means a difference in slopes, so the two slopes are compared with the standard error of their difference. Each line uses two degrees of freedom, so ν = 14 + 14 − 4 = 24.

questions.stem: Reaction time is recorded in seconds and the correlation with hours of sleep is r = −0.62. The reaction times are then converted to milliseconds. What happens to the slope b of reaction time on sleep and to r?
options: Both b and r are multiplied by 1000.
b is multiplied by 1000 and r stays −0.62.
b stays the same and r is multiplied by 1000.
Neither b nor r changes.
questions.why: The slope carries the units of y per unit of x, so it scales with the units of y. The correlation has no units because the units cancel in its formula, so it does not change.

notes: All data are invented. Hand cases give raw (x, y) pairs in the table and the eight useful summations in the context sentence, written with lowercase x and y to match the formula notation of the reference cases.
Step-level table lookups use the key classTable, as the reference session 18 cases do. The case-level key is lookup.

n18-slow-wave-sleep-retention and n18-amphetamine-locomotion-sex carry two extra keys, rOutput and rCode (the keys used by the session 20 reference cases), holding summary(lm()) printouts. The printouts were built from statsmodels fits and formatted to imitate R, so they were not produced by R itself. The raw data behind them are embedded in check_session18a.py, which refits them and checks the printed coefficients.
As in the reference cases, the two R-output cases calculate from the rounded printed coefficients, so results differ slightly from full-precision fits.

n18-amphetamine-locomotion-sex keeps the reference key names (nM, nF, bM, sbM, bF, sbF, femaleXbar, femaleSx, critical002, pooled...). It adds critical01, which holds the 0.01 column value 2.763 used for the P range 0.01 < P < 0.02. Both groups share the same doses, so the pooled standard error equals the equal-n standard error up to rounding of the printed values.
n18-cortisol-digit-span is the case where the trend is not significant (|t| = 1.257 < 2.306). Its P-range step reports P > 0.05 after checking the 0.20 column.
n18-p300-latency-development has n = 11 (row 9) and n18-reading-speed-age has n = 12. All degrees of freedom (8, 9, 16, 28) are printed rows, so no bracketing was needed.
The prediction points are not data values. These are 65 yr in n18-age-hearing-threshold, 6.8 syll/s in n18-speech-rate-recognition and 90 min in n18-slow-wave-sleep-retention.
Slope and predict hand cases have more steps than the reference cases because the line and s_y|x must first be calculated from the summations.

Wording review. Each hand-case context now carries the homework sentence "Note: some useful summations have already been calculated for you below, which you can use.", followed by "The summations are ...". Negative numbers in running text use the minus sign − as the reference cases do. check_session18a.py was adjusted to read the summations after the new sentence and to allow that one colon in the context.
